A dedicated public page presents image generation.
A dedicated public page presents video generation.
A dedicated public page presents voice (voice mode / dictation / realtime).
A public page describes the desktop app truthfully (what it does, availability, download).
A public page describes the mobile app and its availability.
A public page tells a visitor how to install the CLI and offers a working install.
A public page describes the IDE extension and its availability.
A public page describes the browser extension and its availability.
A logged-out visitor can browse and search a directory of available integrations.
A logged-out visitor can browse the plugin catalogue read from the live registry, with a path to install.
A logged-out visitor can browse a public directory of skills.
A public gallery offers curated starting templates a visitor can preview and launch into chat.
A public directory lists custom assistants / agents a visitor can browse.
Each integration has its own public detail page.
Each plugin has a public detail page with description, permissions, install info and release history.
Each template has its own previewable page (addressable URL).
A public pricing page lists individual plans with prices and lets a visitor buy one; its plan copy matches enforcement.
A public page shows Team per-seat pricing and lets a buyer choose seats and purchase.
A public page presents the Enterprise offering with a sales path.
A plan-comparison table lists plans against features, and each cell matches enforcement.
Public pages explain how managed usage, allowances and credits work.
A download page offers installers per platform/architecture, reporting what is actually published.
A public changelog lists dated releases.
Individual product announcements have their own public pages.
A public documentation portal indexes guides and API docs.
A public help centre offers searchable articles.
A public service-status page shows current health from live checks.
A public trust and security centre explains security posture and data handling.
An About view gives product and company information.
A contact / support page lets a visitor reach the company.
A form lets a prospect request an Enterprise conversation and the request is stored.
Partners and developers can submit a listing or partnership application through a form.

text: Privacy, terms, cookies, and accessibility pages.

A visitor can choose language and region on the public site.
A logged-out visitor opening a public share link sees the shared content.
The surface offers a sign-in entry that authenticates the user to their AGI account, in-app or through a browser/device handoff that returns a session to the surface.
A new user can create an account (email or provider) from a sign-up screen on the surface, or is handed to one.
After sign-up the user must confirm their email address on a verification screen before the account is usable.
A code-entry field accepts an emailed or authenticator code (with resend and one-time-code autofill) and verifies it.
The user can sign in by clicking an emailed link and sees a confirmation that the link signed them in.
From sign-in the user can request a password reset and receives a reset code or link by email.
After verifying the reset code the user sets a new password and is signed in.
Sign-in and sign-up offer social providers (e.g. Google, GitHub) that complete sign-in on this surface.
A user of an SSO-enabled organization can start enterprise single sign-on from the sign-in screen and land signed in.
Entering a work email discovers the organization's sign-in by the email domain and routes the user to it.
A signed-in user can register a passkey for their account and see it listed (with rename/removal).
A user with a registered passkey can sign in with it instead of a password or code.
A user can enroll an authenticator (QR + setup key, confirm code, backup codes) and from then on sign-in asks for that second factor.
At sign-in an account with MFA is challenged for its second factor (with alternatives such as backup codes) before a session is issued.
When MFA is enabled (or codes are regenerated) the user is shown one-time recovery codes once and can copy, print or download them.
A user who has lost their password, email or second factor can start and complete an account-recovery flow that restores access.
A signed-in user can link another sign-in method (e.g. Google, GitHub) to the same account and see or unlink linked methods.
When sign-up or provider sign-in hits an existing account (or sign-in hits none), the user is told and offered the right path (sign in instead, or create).
Before first use the user reviews and accepts the current Terms (versioned), acceptance is recorded, and a terms change re-prompts.

text: Age or eligibility verification where applicable.
criterion: Where age limits apply, the user must confirm age or eligibility before use, and under-age users are blocked or restricted.
During onboarding the user sets up basic profile details (at least the name the assistant uses) and they are saved to the account.
During setup the user can choose or confirm their language and time zone (or they are detected and shown for change).
Onboarding asks the user their role or intended use and uses the answer (e.g. to tailor replies or suggestions).
Onboarding lets the user set personalization (name to use, what they do, preferred style) that then shapes replies.
During setup the user is told about memory and chooses whether and how it is used, with the choice changeable later.
The user can bring memories or history over from another assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) through a guided import flow.
New users are shown a few recommended apps/connectors (e.g. based on their role) and can connect them in a guided flow.
New users are offered recommended plugins/skills and can install them in a guided step.
The app walks the user through the local permissions it needs (folders, commands, screen control) with guidance, and records the grants.
The browser extension can be paired with the desktop app (or account) through a guided code/confirm step, with a way to unpair.
A phone can be paired with the desktop app by QR or short code, and the pairing is bound to the signed-in account.
The user is offered an optional, declinable way to turn on notifications (primer or setup step), and can change it later.
A user can compare plans and select one, reaching a real purchase for the chosen plan.
A user can start a trial of a paid plan, sees it marked as a trial, and the trial ends (reverts or bills) on schedule.
New users get an introduction to their first conversation (what to try, how it works) that leads into a first chat.
New users get a checklist of setup steps whose progress is saved, so they can leave and resume it later.
Without an account the user can try the product (guest/local use), and later sign up with their guest work carried over or still available.
Signed-in user lands on (or opens) an empty new-chat screen with a ready composer from which a new conversation starts.
Opening a past conversation (from the list or a link) shows its transcript and lets the user continue it.
A search destination where the user types a keyword, gets past conversations matching titles or message text, and opens one.
A destination lists the user's archived conversations and lets them open, restore or delete them.
Conversations the user pinned are shown together in a pinned section or filter and open from there.
A Projects destination lists the user's projects and lets them open or create one.
Opening a project shows its home: name, description/instructions summary, and entry points to its chats and files.
Within a project, a list of the project's conversations that open when selected.
Within a project, a files/sources view lists the project's knowledge files and lets the user add and remove them.
A place to view and edit a project's instructions, which then apply to chats in that project.
A project members view shows who has access to a project and lets the owner add or remove people.
A project memory view shows what has been remembered for that project, with scope controls, separately from account memory.
A home for agentic work where the user states a goal for an autonomous multi-step (AGI Work) run and can reach their recent work.
A dashboard lists the user's active/running work tasks with their live status, filterable from finished ones.
Opening one task shows its status, step-by-step activity/transcript, outputs, and any pending decision.
An approvals inbox gathers every pending approval across the user's tasks and lets them approve or reject each.
A scheduled-task manager lists the user's schedules with cadence/status and lets them create, edit, pause/resume, run now and delete.
Opening one routine/schedule shows its configuration (prompt, cadence, next run) and its run history.
A coding home lists the user's coding sessions and starts a new one on a repository or runtime.
A coding-session workspace shows the session transcript, file changes/diffs and a composer to steer the next turn.
A devices destination lists the user's linked devices with status/last activity and lets them manage (rename, unlink, pair) them.
A viewer opens a session running on another of the user's devices and shows its live transcript/state with controls.
A Library destination lists everything the account produced or uploaded (files, images, videos, documents, artifacts) with filters and open/download actions.
A destination lists resources (projects, conversations, artifacts, connectors) that other people shared with the user, and opens them.
An artifact gallery lists the user's generated artifacts and opens any of them.
An artifact editor lets the user edit an artifact's content directly and saves the result as a new version.
A dedicated image studio where the user writes a prompt, picks style/size options, generates images and sees results/history in one place.
An image collection view shows all images the user generated or uploaded, with open/download/remix actions.
A dedicated video studio where the user prompts, configures and generates videos and sees results/history in one place.
A media job history lists image/video generation jobs with their status (queued, running, failed, done) and links to results.
A notebook workspace holds a set of sources and notes that the user reads, annotates and chats over, with generated outputs (NotebookLM-style).
A research report reader lists the user's research reports and opens one with its sections and cited sources.
A signed-in destination lists the user's custom assistants (GPT/Gem-style) and lets them open, create, edit and delete them.
A builder lets the user define a custom assistant (name, instructions, knowledge, tools, starters), preview it and save it.
A skills manager lists installed and available skills and lets the user install, enable/disable, author and remove them.
A plugins manager lists installed and available plugins and lets the user install, configure, update and remove them.
A connected-accounts destination lists the third-party services the user has connected and lets them connect, reconnect and disconnect each.
A model catalog lists the models the user can reach with capabilities/context/price and lets them pick one or set a default.
A usage dashboard shows current usage against plan limits per window (session/weekly/credits), reset times and recent usage history.
A billing settings destination shows the current plan, renewal, payment method and invoices, and lets the user change or cancel the plan.
A personal settings destination lets the signed-in user view and change their own preferences (profile, appearance, personalization, notifications) and saves them.
A workspace administration destination lets an admin manage members, roles, invitations, policies and workspace settings.
A developer console lets the user create/revoke API keys, see API usage per key, read API docs and try requests.
A help-and-feedback destination links to help/docs/status and lets the user send product feedback or a bug report from inside the product.
A persistent top header shows where the user is (brand/conversation title) and the primary actions for the current view.
A control lets the user switch between product areas or modes (chat, projects, code, work, etc.) from the shell.
The user can switch between two or more signed-in accounts without signing out.
From the shell, the user can see the active workspace and switch between personal and team workspaces.
A control collapses the navigation sidebar to a rail (or hides it) and expands it again.
A drag handle lets the user resize the navigation sidebar width, and the width persists.
The navigation sidebar has a search entry that filters or searches conversations.
A persistent New chat action starts a fresh conversation from anywhere in the shell.
Pinned items appear in their own section at the top of navigation.
Navigation shows a list of recent conversations that open on selection.
Recent conversations can be shown grouped under their projects in navigation.
Recent conversations are grouped by date buckets (Today, Yesterday, This week, Older).
Each conversation row shows its title, indicates the active one, and opens the conversation.
Navigation shows project rows that open the project (and expose its actions).
Background work/tasks appear as rows marked as tasks (distinct from chats) with their state, and open on selection.
Rows in mixed lists carry an icon (or equivalent marker) that tells the resource type apart (chat, project, task, file) visually and for assistive tech.
Navigation marks items whose task or response is still running, visually and for screen readers.
Navigation marks items that are blocked waiting for the user (approval or input).
Items with new results the user has not seen are marked unread (visually and for assistive tech) and clear when opened.
Each row has an overflow (⋯) menu with its actions (share, rename, pin, archive, move, delete).
A row can be renamed in place (inline field, Enter to save, Escape to cancel) and the new title persists.
The user can drag rows (e.g. pinned items or projects) to reorder them, and the order persists.
The user can drag a conversation onto a project in navigation to move it there.
Nested app views show a breadcrumb trail back to their parents (e.g. Projects / Project / Chat).
Back and forward navigation move through the user's in-app history.
A global command palette (keyboard-invoked) searches and runs app commands and destinations.
A keyboard-shortcut help view lists the available shortcuts and is reachable from the app.
A notification center lists account notifications, shows an unread count, and lets the user open and mark them read.
A user/profile menu shows who is signed in and offers account actions (settings, plan, sign out).
A help menu gathers help centre, support contact, feedback and shortcuts in one place.
A visible Upgrade entry in the shell takes an eligible user into the plan upgrade flow.
A status indicator shows whether the app is connected to its backend/runtime and offers reconnect when not.
When the device loses network, a visible offline indicator appears and clears when back online.
The app tells the user when a new release is available (or just installed) and how to get it.
On narrow screens navigation lives in a slide-in drawer opened from a header button, with focus management and dismissal.
On phones a persistent bottom navigation bar switches between the main areas.
On tablet widths navigation and content sit side by side (persistent or rail sidebar) instead of a phone drawer.
Each resource (conversation, project, task) has a stable link that opens it directly in the app.
Routes show a loading state while resolving and a clear not-found/unavailable screen for missing or forbidden resources.
The surface paints page and panel backgrounds from named semantic background tokens, per theme, not per-component literals.
Raised surfaces (cards, menus, popovers, dialogs) use a named elevated-surface token distinct from the page ground in each theme.
Primary and muted text use named text tokens that meet 4.5:1 on every surface they land on, without opacity dilution.
Borders and dividers use named border/rule tokens (subtle and strong) per theme.
Accent and selection colours have separate fill, text and on-fill roles that each meet contrast on the backgrounds they are drawn on.

text: Success, warning, error, and information colors.
criterion: Success, warning, error and info each have text and fill roles, and status text meets 4.5:1 on its background in both themes.
The surface declares its UI (sans), editorial and monospace font families once and loads the faces it names.
Headings use one defined heading scale (named levels pairing size, weight and line-height) applied across the surface.
Body text uses a defined base size (and small variant) applied consistently, respecting the user's text-size preference where offered.
Captions and metadata use a named small-text role no smaller than 12px that keeps AA contrast.
Code and technical text use a declared monospace family and size distinct from body text.
Line height is defined per text role (paired with size) rather than set ad hoc per element.
Rendered paragraphs in responses are separated by a defined vertical gap set in one rule.
Lists in rendered content use a defined indentation (and nesting step).
Code blocks have defined internal padding set in one shared rule.
Table cells (in rendered content and data tables) have defined, consistent padding.
Consecutive conversation turns are separated by one defined vertical spacing value.
The per-message action toolbar sits a defined distance below the message it belongs to.
The composer has defined internal padding around the input and its controls.
Pages use defined page-edge gutters that step with viewport width.
Sidebar/history list rows have one defined row height.
Menu items share one defined item height/padding across menus.
Dialogs and sheets share one defined inner padding.
Form fields share a defined label-to-input and field-to-field spacing.
Icons come from one family with a fixed grid and stroke width, sized from a small set.
Buttons come in a defined set of sizes/densities from one component.
Corner radii come from one named radius ladder.
Shadows come from a small named elevation scale per theme.
Stacking order uses one named z-index ladder; components never invent numeric layers.
Animations and transitions use named durations and easing curves.
When the user asks for reduced motion (OS setting or in-app), looping and travelling animation stops or is replaced with a gentle equivalent.
The user can use light, dark, or follow-the-system appearance, and the whole surface (including code) follows it.
A high-contrast treatment exists (OS setting and/or in-app) that strengthens text, borders and focus.

text: Selected, focused, hovered, pressed, and disabled states.
criterion: Interactive controls show distinct selected, focused, hovered, pressed and disabled states.
The surface ships its brand mark and application icons at the sizes the platform needs.
An empty new chat shows its start view (greeting, prompt entry or suggestions) centred in the available area rather than an empty transcript.
Message text is constrained to a readable column width that stays centred when the window is wide.
Data work (tables, charts, spreadsheets) can be viewed in a layout that uses the full window width instead of the reading column.
An artifact opens in its own pane beside the conversation so both are visible and usable at once.
Sources behind an answer open in an inspector pane beside the conversation, so the reader can check a source without leaving the transcript.
A live web page is shown beside the conversation, so the user can watch or use the page while chatting about it.
A coding session shows the conversation alongside the code workspace (changes, diffs, terminal or editor) in one view.
Two or more live sessions are visible side by side in one window, each independently usable.
Several live sessions can be stacked one above another in one window, each independently usable.
The user can drag (or keyboard-adjust) the width of the left navigation sidebar.
The right-hand inspector pane can be resized by drag or keyboard, and the conversation reflows.
Secondary navigation (conversation list, menus) can be collapsed out of the way and reopened.
Panels can be moved to a different edge or region of the window (docked) and stay there.
A panel of the desktop app can be torn off into its own OS window and used there.
An editor (prompt, document or source) can take over the whole screen for focused editing and return to the chat.
A long report (e.g. a research report) can be read in a full-screen reading view.
An image or video in the conversation can be opened in a full-screen viewer and dismissed back to the chat.
A small always-on-top companion window can float over other apps or pages and be summoned without switching to the main app.
A compact companion mode shows a reduced chat UI (no sidebar or side panels) sized for quick questions.
The composer stays anchored at the bottom of the chat while the transcript scrolls above it.
The composer grows (or opens a larger editor) as a long prompt is typed, instead of staying one line.

text: Scrollable transcript independent from side panels.
criterion: The transcript scrolls in its own region, so scrolling it does not move side panels, header or composer (and vice versa).
The artifact toolbar (copy, download, view toggles, close) stays visible while the artifact content scrolls.
Table headers stay pinned while a long table scrolls.
On narrow windows, side panels stop sitting beside the conversation and stack over it (overlay or sheet), then return beside it when wide.
On phone-sized screens, menus and pickers open as bottom sheets instead of desktop popovers.
On tablet widths the app shows two columns (navigation plus content) instead of the phone single column.
Content and the composer stay clear of notches/home indicators, and the layout adjusts when the on-screen keyboard opens.
Resizable or responsive panels enforce minimum and maximum widths so neither the panel nor the conversation collapses.
Layout choices the user made (sidebar collapsed, panel widths, open panels) come back on the next visit.
The desktop window reopens at its last size and position, and stays on screen when the monitor arrangement changes.
Printing a conversation or report produces a print-specific layout: no app chrome, the whole content, paper-friendly colours and sensible page breaks.
The main action in a view uses a visually emphasised primary button style, applied in shipped UI, whose label meets contrast on its fill.
A less prominent secondary (outline/ghost) button style exists and is used beside primary actions in shipped UI.
Irreversible actions use a distinct destructive button style (danger colour before hover) whose label meets contrast.
Icon-only buttons exist in shipped UI and each carries an accessible name (aria-label or equivalent).
A split button (main action plus an attached menu of alternative actions) is used in shipped UI.
A toggle button (a button with an on/off pressed state announced to assistive tech) is used in shipped UI.
Related buttons are grouped into a labelled button group in shipped UI.
Links in text are visibly styled as links and open their destination when activated.
Single-line text inputs with a visible label or accessible name are used in shipped UI.
A multi-line text area that accepts newlines is used in shipped UI (e.g. the composer).
A search field (search semantics, placeholder or label, filters as typed or on submit) is used in shipped UI.
Secret entry (passwords, API keys, tokens) uses a masked field in shipped UI.
A one-time-code field (short numeric code, one-time-code autofill or paste) is used where the product asks for a code.
Checkboxes (independent on/off choices in a list, with checked state exposed) are used in shipped UI.
A radio group (mutually exclusive options, all visible, with checked state exposed) is used in shipped UI.
Switches (immediate on/off settings with switch semantics) are used in shipped UI.
A segmented control (a small set of mutually exclusive options shown as joined segments) is used in shipped UI.
A single-select menu (choose one value from a list) is used in shipped UI.
A searchable combobox (type to filter a list, then pick one, with listbox semantics or keyboard navigation) is used in shipped UI.
A multiselect control (pick several values from one list, each selection shown and removable) is used in shipped UI.
A token/chip input (typed entries become removable chips inside or beside the field) is used in shipped UI.
A numeric stepper (number field with increment/decrement) is used in shipped UI.
A slider (drag or arrow keys to set one value on a scale) is used in shipped UI.
A range slider (two thumbs selecting a minimum and maximum) is used in shipped UI.
A date picker (calendar or native date control) is used where a date is entered in shipped UI.
A time picker (native or custom time control) is used where a time is entered in shipped UI.
A time zone picker (searchable list of zones, defaulting to the device zone) is used where schedules take a zone.
A colour picker (swatches or a colour input) is used where the user chooses a colour.
A file input (choose files from the device) is used in shipped UI.
An upload drop zone accepts files dragged onto it and shows a drag-over state.
Tabs (a tablist switching between panels, with the selected tab exposed) are used in shipped UI.
An accordion (a stack of sections that expand and collapse, each with a labelled header) is used in shipped UI.
A disclosure control (a toggle that shows or hides one block of detail, exposing its expanded state) is used in shipped UI.
Dropdown menus (a button that opens a list of actions with menu keyboard behaviour) are used in shipped UI.
A context menu (right-click or long-press opens actions for the item under the pointer) is used in shipped UI.
A nested menu (a menu item that opens a submenu) is used in shipped UI.
Tooltips (short labels shown on hover or focus for controls) are used in shipped UI.
Popovers (anchored floating panels that open from a trigger and dismiss on Escape or outside click) are used in shipped UI.
Hover cards (a rich preview that appears when hovering a link, mention or citation) are used in shipped UI.
Badges (small status or count markers attached to an item) are used in shipped UI.
Tags (small labels that categorise or describe an item, distinct from status badges) are used in shipped UI.
Message authors are distinguished visually and for assistive technology (R-n: avatar or equivalent marker plus an accessible label).
Progress indicators (determinate bars or indeterminate spinners with an accessible name) are used in shipped UI.
Skeleton placeholders stand in for content while it loads.
Toasts (transient, non-blocking notifications that dismiss themselves) are used in shipped UI.
Inline alerts (a message block inside the content, with alert or status semantics, for warnings or errors) are used in shipped UI.
Banners (a full-width strip at the top or bottom of a view for system or account messages) are used in shipped UI.
Pagination controls (next/previous, page numbers or an explicit "Load more") let the user move through a long list.
Empty states (a message and next step shown when a list or view has no content) are used in shipped UI.
Error states (a view-level message with a recovery action when content fails to load or a request fails) are used in shipped UI.
A picker lists selectable resources (files, projects, models, skills) and narrows the list as the user types a query.
A control lists the available models and switches the conversation to the one the user picks.
Before or while asking, the user can choose which sources (specific sites, files, connected apps) the answer may draw on.
When a connector has more than one linked account, the user can pick which account a task or chat uses.
The user can see their personal and team workspaces in a list and switch the active one.
The user can pick one of their projects so the chat or task runs in that project.
The user can choose which code repository a coding session works in, from a list or by URL/path.
The user can pick the branch a coding session starts from or works on from a list of the repository's branches.
The user can pick which device is used (microphone, speaker, camera or paired computer) from a list.
When granting access (an API key, tool approvals or site automation), the user chooses how far the permission reaches: which capabilities, or once versus always.
The user can pick one or more people (workspace members or recipients) by name or email to share with, invite or assign.
When creating a scheduled task, the user sets how it repeats (once, daily, weekly, monthly or a custom rule) and the schedule runs on that cadence.
The user can browse their stored files (uploads and generated outputs) in a list or grid, open one, and filter or search it.
Files are shown in a nested folder tree the user can expand and collapse to reach a file.
Tabular data is shown in a table with column headers that the user can sort (and scroll) to inspect the rows.
Resources (files, artifacts, projects) are shown as a grid of cards the user can scan and open.
The user can browse their images and videos as a gallery and open one in a larger viewer.
After an image edit, the user can drag a slider over one frame to compare the original and edited images.
The steps of a run are shown in time order, each with its state and (where known) how long it took.
The user can see a feed of recent account events (sign-ins, changes, runs), newest first.
Tasks are laid out as a board with a column per status so the user sees and manages work by stage.
A multi-step flow shows which step the user is on out of how many (e.g. dots or "Step 2 of 4") and advances or goes back with it.
A guided setup runs as ordered steps that collect the user's choices (name, model, sign-in) and saves them when it finishes.
Two panes sit side by side (e.g. chat and artifact) and the user can resize the split, by pointer and by keyboard.
The user can move panels to different positions (left, right, bottom, floating) and the layout keeps that arrangement.
A panel lists a resource's saved versions (when, what) and lets the user open or restore one.
Changes to a file are shown as a diff (added and removed lines marked) that the user can read before accepting.
The user can open an answer's sources and see each one's title, origin and the excerpt it contributed, then open it.
A meter shows how much of the plan allowance is used (per window) with the reset time, readable by assistive tech.
The user sees their purchased credit balance in one place, next to a way to add credits.
One view states in plain language what the assistant or a connected app is allowed to do (scopes, autonomy, allowed sites or tools).
When an action needs consent, an inline card names the action and offers approve and deny, and the choice resumes or stops the run.
Each integration shows a card with its connection state (connected, expired, not connected) and the action to connect or disconnect.
Before sending, a visible notice warns when the chosen model cannot handle something in the request (images, tools, attachments, context size).
A running task shows a card with its current state and progress (steps done, latest action) that updates while it runs.
An answer can embed a widget the user operates in place (choices, map, app card), and the choice or state feeds back into the conversation.
An inbox lists the user's notifications newest first, marks which are unread (visibly and for screen readers), and lets them open or mark them read.
A keyboard shortcut opens a searchable list of commands and destinations; typing filters it and Enter runs the choice.
A create-project dialog (or command) asks for a name and creates the project in the account.
The user opens rename on a conversation, edits the title in a field or prompt, and the new title is saved.
A move dialog or menu lets the user pick a project for a conversation and files it there.
A duplicate action creates an independent copy of a conversation or project and says where the copy is.
Archiving asks to confirm, or confirms afterwards with a way to undo, and says where archived items can be found.
Deleting asks for confirmation that names the item before anything is removed.
An irreversible delete says plainly that it cannot be undone and needs an explicit second confirmation.
A share dialog creates a link to the conversation, shows it for copying, and states who can open it.
The user can share a file (or folder) from their library with someone, by link or the system share sheet.
An artifact share dialog publishes it to a link, lets the user copy it and choose who can open it, and can take it down.
A publish dialog puts a generated app or page on a live URL and hands back the link.
For a shared link the user can see its access (who, expiry) and change or revoke it.
An invite dialog takes an email and role, sends the invitation, and lists pending invites to revoke or renew.
A role dialog changes a member's role after confirmation, and the server enforces the new role.
The owner picks another member and confirms, and ownership moves to them.
A dialog lets the user choose which sources (sites, files, apps) an answer or research run may use.
Choosing upload opens the device file chooser and the picked files attach to the message.
A connect dialog starts the service's real authorization (OAuth or key) and ends with the account connected.
An expired connection offers a reconnect dialog that re-runs authorization and keeps its settings.
When a service has several connected accounts, a dialog lets the user pick which one to use or make default.
An install dialog shows the plugin and installs it into the account or workspace.
Before installing or updating, a dialog lists the permissions the plugin requires and asks the user to accept them.
An update dialog offers a newer plugin version, shows what changes, and applies it.
An import dialog takes a skill file or package and adds a usable skill.
An edit dialog changes a skill's name, description and instructions and saves them.
Switching to a model that cannot handle the conversation (images, tools, context) warns and asks before switching.
As a conversation nears or passes the model's context limit, the user gets a clear warning with what to do (trim, compact, new chat).
When a usage limit is reached, the user sees which limit, when it resets, and what they can do.
From where the limit is hit, a purchase dialog lets the user buy extra credits and completes payment.
An upgrade dialog compares plans (price, limits, features) before the user picks one.
A cancel dialog lets the user cancel their subscription, says when access ends, and confirms.
A payment-method dialog lets the user add or replace the card on file.
Before a sensitive account action, a dialog asks the user to prove it is them (code or passkey) and only then proceeds.
Before or when the microphone is first needed, the product explains why it wants it and what to do if access is refused.
When sharing the screen, the user picks which screen or window to share before anything is captured.
Before the assistant first controls the computer or browser, a dialog says what it will be able to do and the user grants or refuses it.
Before the assistant reads or writes a local folder, the user is asked to grant access to that folder.
When a tool action needs approval, a prompt shows the action and the user approves or denies that one call.
Before private or sensitive data is sent to an outside destination, the user is asked to approve that transfer and told what goes where.
A pairing dialog links a phone or another device to this machine by code or QR, bound to the signed-in account.
Leaving an editor with unsaved edits warns the user and lets them keep editing or discard.
When the same item was changed elsewhere, the user sees both versions and chooses which to keep (or merges).
An export dialog lets the user pick a format and exports the conversation or item to a file.
A report dialog lets the user flag an answer (with a reason) and the report reaches moderation.
A feedback dialog, reachable product-wide, sends the user's message to the team's feedback store.
Before diagnostics or crash reports leave the device, the user is told what is included and chooses (or sets a preference that is honoured).
A data-export dialog requests a copy of the account's data and delivers it as a download.
An account-deletion dialog explains what is deleted and requires explicit confirmation before deleting the account.
Every interactive control exposes an accessible name (visible text, aria-label or platform equivalent) that says what it does.
Each screen has a top heading and sections use nested headings, so screen-reader users can jump by heading.
Everything can be reached and operated from the keyboard, including menus with arrow keys and Escape.
The focused control always shows a clearly visible focus indicator when navigating by keyboard.
Opening a dialog moves focus into it, Tab stays inside it, and Escape closes it.
Closing a dialog, menu or panel returns focus to the control that opened it.
When something finishes (a reply, a tool step, a save, a connection), a screen reader hears a short announcement without moving focus.
A streaming reply is announced calmly (in word-bounded chunks or once when done), never token by token and never twice.
Tool steps and approval requests expose their state (running, done, failed, waiting for approval) to assistive tech, with labelled approve and deny controls.
Anything revealed on hover is also reachable by touch (always visible on touch screens or shown on tap).
Every drag operation (drop files, resize, reorder) has a non-drag alternative such as a button, menu or arrow keys.
Text scales with the user's text-size setting (browser, OS or app) up to at least 200% without being cut off.
At high browser zoom (400%) the layout reflows to one column with no horizontal scrolling.
With the OS or app reduced-motion preference on, looping and travelling animation stops or is replaced.
Spoken audio (voice conversations) can be shown as live captions.
A voice conversation leaves a readable text transcript kept with the chat.
A chart comes with a text description (title, what is plotted, key values) that assistive tech can read.
A chart can be viewed as a data table (or its data read in order) as an alternative to the graphic.
In a right-to-left language the whole layout mirrors correctly (direction set and spacing uses logical start/end).
Messages mixing left-to-right and right-to-left text render each paragraph in its own direction (e.g. dir="auto").
Typing with an input method (Japanese, Chinese, Korean) never sends the message when Enter confirms a composition.
Dates, times and numbers are formatted for the user's locale rather than a fixed US format.
Prices and money amounts show the right currency symbol and the user's number format.
Counted phrases follow each language's plural rules rather than an English "s" suffix.
Error messages appear in the user's chosen language.
Shortcut hints use the platform's notation (⌘ on Apple, Ctrl elsewhere).
Long labels and longer translated strings wrap or truncate cleanly without overlapping or clipping controls.
The CLI offers a plain output mode for screen readers (no colour, spinners or redraws) and honours NO_COLOR everywhere.
Opening a new chat shows an empty conversation area (no prior messages) with a ready composer.
The new-chat screen greets the signed-in user by their (preferred) name when one is known.

text: Neutral greeting when personalization is disabled.
criterion: When personalization is off (or no name is known), the new-chat greeting is neutral and shows no personal details.
The new-chat screen offers clickable suggested prompts that fill or send a message.
The new-chat screen offers one-tap task-category shortcuts (e.g. write, research, image) that set up the next message.
The new-chat screen offers shortcuts to the user's recent projects that open the project or start a chat in it.
When starting a chat the user is offered their recently used files to attach in one step.
The new-chat screen recommends Skills relevant to the user, which can be applied to the next message.
The new-chat screen recommends apps/connectors worth connecting or using for the next message.
From the new-chat screen the user can explicitly start a web search for the next message.
From the new-chat screen the user can switch on a deep-research mode for the next message.
From the new-chat screen the user can enter an image-creation mode whose send generates an image.
From the new-chat screen the user can enter a video-creation mode whose send starts a video generation.
From the new-chat screen the user can start a spoken (voice-mode) conversation.
From the new-chat screen the user can start agentic (multi-step, tool-using) work rather than a plain chat.
From the new-chat surface the user can start a coding session (a repository/workspace-aware coding agent).
Before or during a new chat the user can switch it to a temporary chat that is not kept in history.
The new-chat screen shows which model the next message will use before the user sends.
The new-chat screen shows which workspace (personal or organization) the new chat will belong to.
Before sending, the user can pick the project a new chat will be created in.
The new-chat screen explains the available modes and gives examples of what each is for.
First-time users are shown a short introduction to the product's key features before or at their first chat.
An unsent draft typed in a new chat is restored when the user returns (after navigation or reload).
A signed-out visitor can use the product within stated guest limits and is prompted to sign in to lift them.
The user can type a plain-text message into the composer and send it.
The composer accepts multi-line text (line breaks are kept in the sent message).
The composer grows taller automatically as the text grows, up to a cap, then scrolls.
The user can manually enlarge the composer (an expand control or resize handle) beyond its automatic height.
The user can open the draft in a full-screen (or external) editor and return it to the composer.
A visible send button submits the composed message (and is disabled with a reason when sending is blocked).
While a reply is generating, a stop control ends it (keeping what was produced).
The user can choose in settings whether Enter sends or inserts a newline (e.g. Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to send).
A keyboard shortcut (e.g. Shift+Enter) inserts a newline without sending.
Standard undo/redo shortcuts (Cmd/Ctrl+Z, Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z) revert and reapply edits in the composer.
Pasting from the clipboard inserts text into the composer and turns pasted files/images into attachments.
Pasting formatted (HTML/rich) text yields clean plain text in the composer, without styling or markup.
Pasted source code is recognized and wrapped in a code block (with a way to paste it as plain text).
Very long input is handled deliberately (turned into an attachment, collapsed, or clearly limited with feedback) instead of flooding the composer.

text: Character or token indicators where useful.
criterion: Where length matters, the composer shows a character or token/context indicator before sending.
The unsent composer text is saved automatically while typing, so it survives a reload or crash.
After a reload, crash or failed send, the unsent text is put back in the composer (with a notice).
Each conversation keeps its own unsent draft; switching chats never carries text into another chat.
In the terminal, Up/Down (and a search key) recall previously sent prompts into the composer.
The product offers prompt suggestions (e.g. follow-up questions) that the user can pick to fill or send the next message.
The user can insert a saved prompt template (e.g. a custom command) into the composer, filling in their own text.
Typing "/" opens a filtered list of commands that can be chosen with keyboard or pointer.
The user can explicitly invoke a Skill from the composer so the next message runs with it.
The user can address a message to a specific agent or assistant by mentioning or selecting it in the composer.
Typing a mention in the composer can reference a project, scoping the message to it.
Typing a mention in the composer can reference a file, whose contents are included with the message.
Typing a mention in the composer can reference a folder, whose contents are made available to the message.
Typing a mention in the composer can reference a code repository (e.g. a connected GitHub repo) as context.
The user can reference an open browser tab (choosing which one) as context for the message.
The user can reference a connected app (connector/MCP server) or one of its resources inline in the composer.
Context attached to the next message (skill, project, folder, files, page) shows as removable chips in the composer.
Sources chosen for the next message (e.g. web search, connector resources, a page) are shown as chips before sending.
Tools switched on for the next message (e.g. research, code, office files) are shown as chips near the composer.
Before sending, the user can choose the output format for the reply (e.g. table, document, code, slides).
A "+" (attach) menu in the composer lists the ways to add files, media and context.
A microphone control dictates speech into the composer text (without sending) for review.
A control starts a hands-free voice conversation (speak, hear the reply) from the composer.
While a reply is still generating, the user can type and queue the next message, which sends when the reply finishes.
A queued message can be edited or cancelled before it is sent.
While an agent is working, the user can send guidance that steers the running task without stopping it.

text: Separate side question that does not modify the main task.
criterion: The user can ask a side question that is answered without being added to (or changing) the main task.
The composer opens the device file chooser and the chosen file is attached to the next message.
Dropping files onto the chat attaches them to the next message.
Pasting an image from the clipboard into the composer attaches it as an image.
The composer offers a camera control that takes a photo and attaches it.
The user can pick one or more photos from the photo library and attach them.
A composer control captures the screen and attaches the screenshot to the next message.
The user can pick a single application window and attach a capture of it.
The user can attach a web page by its URL so its content is used as context for the message.
The user can browse a cloud drive (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox) from the composer and attach a file from it.
The user can pick a file already in their product Library and attach it to a message.
The user can attach a code repository (e.g. a GitHub repo) as the context for a task.
The user can attach a whole folder so the assistant can use the files inside it.
The user can attach an audio file (e.g. MP3, M4A, WAV) and the model receives it.
The user can attach a video file and the model receives it.
One pick action can select several files, and all of them are attached.
An attached image shows a small visual thumbnail in the composer before sending.
Each non-image attachment shows an icon matching its file type (PDF, spreadsheet, code, other).
Each attachment shows its file name and size before sending.
While a file uploads, its chip shows that the upload is in progress.
After upload, the attachment shows that its content is being read or extracted, until it is ready.
A file added to searchable knowledge shows indexing progress and whether indexing finished or failed.
The composer makes clear when an attachment is ready and the message can be sent with it.
When only part of a file could be read or it was cut to a size limit, the user is told.
Adding a file type the chat cannot read shows a notice naming the file and why.
A password-protected file produces a notice that says it is locked and how to fix it.
A failed upload offers Retry on that file, which uploads it again.
While a file is uploading the user can cancel that upload.
Each attachment can be removed before sending, and a removed file is not sent.
An attached file can be replaced with another in place, keeping its position, without removing and re-adding.
Before sending, the user can open an attachment to view it at full size or read its content.
Adding the same file twice is detected and handled visibly (skipped, merged or flagged) rather than sent twice silently.
When a file fails, the error is shown against that file (name and reason), not as one generic message.
After adding several files at once the user sees one summary of what was attached and what was refused.
The composer explains whether and how long attached files are kept.
If the selected model cannot read an attached file type, the composer warns before sending and offers a fix.
When a file cannot go the normal way, the user is told the alternative (switch model or mode, convert, or what is sent instead).
The composer always shows the name of the model the next message will use.
Each model in the selector shows which provider or developer makes it.
Models are grouped by family (e.g. all versions of one model line together) so related models sit side by side.
The user can type to filter the model list by name.
The user can mark models as favourites and see them together at the top.
The selector lists the models the user used most recently.
The selector highlights a short list of recommended models for the user.
The user can choose Auto so the product picks a model per message.
The user can set which model or profile new chats start with, as a lasting default.
The user can pick a specific model and the next message uses it.
Each model in the selector has a short description of what it is good for.
Models show which inputs they accept (e.g. images, audio) as badges.
Models show which outputs they produce (e.g. image, video, audio) as badges.
Models show whether they can use tools.
The selector shows how much context each model can hold.
The selector tells the user which models are faster or slower.
The selector shows how much each model costs or how fast it uses up the allowance.
Models the user's plan cannot use are marked with the plan that unlocks them.
Preview or experimental models carry a visible badge in the selector.
A model scheduled for retirement shows a notice with its leaving date before it disappears.
A model that is temporarily unavailable is marked as such in the selector and cannot be picked by mistake.
For reasoning models the user can choose how hard the model thinks (effort level).
Where a model offers a faster serving tier, the user can turn it on.
The user can set a preferred response length (shorter or longer answers).
Where sampling settings are exposed, the user can set them (temperature, top-p).
Where a model is offered by several providers, the user can choose which provider serves it.
The user can pick a model that runs on their own device.
The user can choose to send turns through their own provider key, supplied in the product.
The chosen model is remembered for the next session.
A conversation can keep its own model, separate from the default used elsewhere.
The user can run a single turn with a different model without changing the conversation's model.
Each answer shows which model actually produced it.
When a different model answered because the chosen one failed or was unavailable, the answer says so and why.
Switching to a model that cannot handle the current conversation (images, tools, context) asks for confirmation and explains what will be lost.
When the chosen model cannot read attached files, the user can choose to keep them (switching to a model that can) or remove them.
The author of each turn is distinguishable visually (avatar, name, alignment/bubble style or terminal marker) AND announced to assistive tech (R-n).
The text the user sent is shown in their message in the transcript.
Files and images sent with a user turn are listed on that message (thumbnail or named chip) after sending.
A sent user message shows chips for the non-file context it carried (quoted text, connector/MCP resources, page, editor selection, @mentions).
Each user message exposes when it was sent (inline or on demand).
A user message that was edited after sending is visibly marked as edited.
A sent user message offers a Copy action that puts its text on the clipboard.
A sent user message can be edited in place and resubmitted, producing a new reply.
A sent user message can be re-sent unchanged from the message itself to get a fresh reply.
From a chosen user message the user can start a new branch conversation that contains the thread up to that message.
When a user message has several revisions the user can page between them (n of m) and the thread follows the chosen revision.
A long user message is shown collapsed with a control that expands it to full length.
An expanded long user message can be collapsed again.
While a user message is not yet accepted by the service, the message shows a pending/sending/queued state.
When a user message fails to deliver, the transcript shows a clear failed state for that turn.
A failed send offers Retry that re-sends the same turn (text and attachments) and replaces the failure with the new outcome.
A message sent while a reply is still running is shown as queued (not yet sent) until it goes out.
Unsent composer text is kept as a draft per conversation, separate from sent messages, and a failed send returns to the composer as an unsent draft.
A user message that came from speech is marked as a voice transcript (e.g. mic badge or "Transcribed").
Messages brought in from elsewhere (another product, a shared link, another device) are marked with where they came from.
In a conversation with several human participants, each user message shows which person wrote it.
A user can obtain and open a link that lands on one specific message in a conversation.
Assistant turns are distinguishable from the user's visually and to assistive tech, ideally naming the assistant/model (R-n).
The answer body renders incrementally as tokens arrive, with markdown formatting.
While the assistant works and before/while text arrives, a visible (and announced) working indicator is shown.
An answer offers a collapsible summary of the model's reasoning and/or the work it did (steps, tools), expandable on demand.
Tool calls made for the answer appear in a tool-activity section with each tool's name, status and result.
Claims in an answer carry citation markers that link to the sources the answer used.
A finished answer that used sources ends with a sources footer/list the user can open.
Files the assistant produced appear as cards on the answer with name/type and open/download.
An answer that created an artifact shows a card that opens the artifact viewer/panel.
Images the assistant generated or returned render inline in the answer (viewable/downloadable).
Audio the assistant produced (speech, music, clips) plays inline in the answer with playback controls.
Videos the assistant generated play inline in the answer with controls and download.
Answers can contain interactive widgets (cards with choices, maps, actions) the user operates in place.
After an answer the product offers relevant follow-up prompts the user can pick.
One action copies the whole answer's text to the clipboard.
A copy action places the answer on the clipboard with its formatting (rich text/HTML) so it pastes formatted into documents.
An answer can be read aloud with text-to-speech from a control on the answer.
While an answer is being read aloud, the user can stop playback from the same place.
A completed answer can be regenerated in place, producing a new attempt for the same prompt.
A failed answer shows a Retry control that re-runs the turn and replaces the failure with the new outcome.
An answer cut off by the output limit offers Continue, which resumes the same answer.
From an answer, the user can regenerate it with a different model in one step.
One action rewrites an answer shorter.
One action rewrites an answer longer/more detailed.
One action rewrites an answer in a different tone.
The user can select part of an answer and ask for that span to be revised or asked about.
From any answer, the user can branch a new conversation that keeps history up to that point and leaves the original unchanged.
When an answer has several attempts, the user can page between them (e.g. '2 of 3').
A thumbs-up on an answer records positive feedback tied to that message.
A thumbs-down on an answer records negative feedback tied to that message.
An answer can be reported (e.g. harmful/incorrect) to the trust-and-safety intake from the answer itself.
The user can share an answer or the conversation (link or system share sheet).
From an answer, the user can save it into a Project's knowledge/sources.
From an answer, the user can save it as an editable document inside the product.
A single answer can be exported to a file (e.g. PDF, Markdown, text).
For each answer the user can see which model actually answered and its usage (tokens/cost/time).
When an answer fails after producing some output, the partial output is kept and visibly marked incomplete, with the reason.
When the model/safety layer refuses, the answer shows a distinct refusal state (not a generic error or a normal answer), with a next step.
An answer the user stopped (or that was interrupted) is marked as stopped, keeps what arrived, and offers to try again.
A turn that returns nothing shows an explicit 'no response' error with retry, not an empty bubble.
A new conversation gets a meaningful title automatically without the user naming it.
The user can rename a conversation and the new title persists.
A conversation can be pinned so it stays at the top of the list, and unpinned.
A conversation can be archived (hidden, kept) and later restored.
A conversation can be deleted, with confirmation, and it disappears everywhere.
A conversation can be duplicated into a new, independent conversation.
An existing conversation can be moved into a Project.
A conversation can be copied into a Project while the original stays where it is.
Within a conversation, the user can switch its working mode (e.g. chat vs agent/work/plan) and later turns follow it.

text: Change privacy mode through an explicit flow.
criterion: The user switches a conversation's privacy mode (e.g. temporary/incognito, local-only) through an explicit flow that explains the consequence.
The user can search within the open conversation's messages.
In-conversation search moves between matches (next/previous) and scrolls to each.
A long conversation offers an outline (list of turns/headings) to see its structure.
The user can jump directly to a chosen earlier turn in the conversation.
After scrolling up, one control returns the view to the latest message.
Leaving and returning to a conversation restores the previous scroll position.
A conversation with branches lets the user see and switch between branches.
The whole conversation can be exported to a file (e.g. Markdown, PDF, JSON).
The user can share a conversation (e.g. a read-only link) from the conversation.
The user can see and revoke links they have shared.
A conversation details view shows its metadata (created/updated, model, message count, id, project).
The user can inspect what context and sources the conversation is using (files, instructions, memory, token budget).
The conversation shows a usage summary (tokens/cost) for the conversation as a whole.
The user can set instructions that apply only to this conversation.
Tool enablement (web search, code, etc.) can be set for this conversation and persists across its turns.
The user can choose which connected accounts/connectors this conversation may use.

text: Active tasks associated with the conversation.
criterion: The conversation shows the active tasks/runs started from it and their status.
A conversation started on one device can be continued on another.
Right after sending, the surface shows that the request was accepted and work has started (before any output).
A request that cannot start yet (queued behind a running turn or a server queue) is shown as waiting/queued.
Before the model answers, the surface shows it is preparing (reading context/attachments/memory).
While the assistant searches sources, the surface shows a searching state (ideally with the query).
While code runs, the surface shows a running-code state for that step.
While a connected service (connector/MCP tool) is called, the surface names the service and shows the call in progress.
When a step needs the user's approval, the turn visibly pauses in a waiting-for-approval state with approve/deny controls.
When the assistant needs information from the user mid-task, it shows a waiting-for-input state with a way to answer.
The moment the first output arrives, the waiting indicator gives way to the answer.
Text appears progressively while the model streams.
Structured output (markdown lists, tables, code blocks) renders correctly while it is still streaming.
While an artifact/file is being produced, the surface shows it is being built.
While an image/video is generated, the surface shows generation progress.
After output completes, the surface shows results being saved/synced and when they are saved.
A finished turn is clearly shown as completed (indicator stops; completion is announced/labelled).
A run that finished with some steps failed is shown as partially completed, distinct from success and failure.
After the user presses stop, the surface shows the stop is in progress until it takes effect.
A stopped turn ends in a clear cancelled/stopped state that keeps what arrived.
When the connection drops mid-turn, the surface shows it is reconnecting and resumes when possible.
Work that was already running is picked up again (after reconnect/reopen) and shown as resuming rather than restarting.
A rate-limited turn says so, with when to retry if known.
A turn blocked by an exhausted budget/plan limit says so and points to the fix (upgrade/usage).
A turn that fails because sign-in expired says so and offers to sign in again.
When a step needs a device that is offline (e.g. the user's desktop or local runtime), the turn shows it is waiting for / cannot reach that device.
When the model provider is down/unavailable, the turn says so and offers retry or another model.
A turn that fails because of the user's input (too long, bad attachment) explains what to change so the user can fix and resend.
A turn that fails after producing useful output keeps that output and marks the failure.
After the app restarts, the conversation and each turn's final state (done/failed/stopped) come back as they were.

text: Background work continuing after UI closure.
criterion: Work keeps running after the UI is closed and its result is there (or resumes) when the user returns.
Assistant text separated by blank lines renders as distinct paragraphs with spacing.
ATX headings (# to ######) render as styled headings, not literal hash marks.
**bold**, *italic* and ~~strikethrough~~ render with the matching text styles.
Numbered lists render with their numbers (respecting the start value) and list indentation.
Bulleted lists render with bullet markers and indentation.
Indented sub-lists render nested under their parent item with deeper indentation.
GFM task items (- [ ] / - [x]) render as checkboxes reflecting their state.
Lines starting with > render as an indented, visually distinct quotation block.
A thematic break (---, ***) renders as a horizontal divider.
`inline code` renders in a monospace style distinct from prose.
Fenced code blocks render as a monospace block preserving whitespace.
[text](url) renders as a link the reader can see and follow.
A bare URL in the answer (https://…, www.…) becomes a clickable link.
Footnote references ([^1]) render as superscript markers linked to a footnotes section.
GFM pipe tables render as a grid with a header row and aligned cells.
A table wider than the answer column scrolls horizontally instead of overflowing or being cut off.
A rendered table offers a one-click action that copies the table (e.g. as TSV/CSV/Markdown).
A rendered table offers a download (CSV/XLSX) of its contents.
Inline LaTeX ($…$ or \(…\)) renders as typeset math inside the sentence.
Display LaTeX ($$…$$ or \[…\]) renders as a centred typeset block.
Backslash-escaped Markdown/math delimiters (\*, \$, \_) display as the literal character without the backslash.
While a reply streams, the partial text renders as formatted Markdown progressively rather than raw syntax until completion.
An unclosed ``` fence mid-stream renders as a code block (not prose) until the closing fence arrives.
Raw HTML/script embedded in model output is sanitized or shown inertly; nothing executes.
External links open outside the app with safe attributes and unsafe schemes (javascript:, data:) are refused.
A reader can drag-select text continuously across paragraphs, lists and code in one answer.
Searching finds text inside an answer and highlights the matching words in the rendered answer.
Printing or exporting an answer/conversation keeps the rendered formatting (headings, lists, tables, code, math).
Right-to-left text (Arabic, Hebrew) renders right-aligned in the correct direction.
A block the renderer cannot draw (unknown card, failed diagram, unknown language) degrades to a readable fallback instead of vanishing or breaking the message.
Each code block shows its language name in a header.
Code is syntax-highlighted according to its language.
Each code block has a copy control that copies exactly its code.
A code block can be downloaded as a source file with a sensible extension.
Code blocks can show line numbers.
The reader can toggle long code lines between wrapping and horizontal scroll.
Long code blocks are collapsed with a control to expand/collapse them.
A code block can be opened in a full-screen/expanded view.
Changed lines in a code suggestion are visually highlighted (added/removed).
Diffs render with diff formatting (+/- lines coloured, hunks readable).
A line referenced by an execution error or diagnostic is highlighted in the code.
The user can have code run (sandbox or local) from the chat and see it execute.
Where multiple runtimes exist, the user can choose the runtime/language for execution.
Before running, the user can supply input parameters or stdin.
Execution stdout is shown in a dedicated output panel under the code.
Standard error is shown separately (and visibly distinguished) from stdout.
Each execution shows how long it took.
Each execution shows its outcome/exit status (success, failure with code).
Files produced by execution are listed and can be opened or downloaded.
Plots/images produced by execution render inline.
A failed or finished execution can be re-run in place.
A running execution can be stopped by the user.
The user can reset the execution runtime/state.
A code block offers an Explain action that asks for an explanation of that code.
A code block can be opened in an editable canvas/editor next to the chat.
A code block can be sent to/opened in the coding workspace (IDE, AGI Code).
Suggested code can be applied to files in the user's repository after review.
When execution installs dependencies, their installation status is shown.
Before or when code runs, the user is told what permission it needs/what it can touch and why.
If the requested runtime/execution is unavailable, the UI states that clearly instead of failing silently.
Answers grounded in sources show citation chips that identify and open the source.
Hovering/tapping a citation shows a preview card (title, site, snippet/date) before opening it.
Web-search results are listed (title, site, link, optional snippet) and can be opened.
News results render as dedicated news cards (headline, outlet, date, image).
Image results render in a swipeable/pageable carousel within the answer.
Video results render as cards with thumbnail, title, duration and play/open.
Audio in an answer (generated speech/music, audio results) plays in an inline audio player.
Charts in answers render interactively (hover/tap values, legend).
The data behind a chart can be inspected (values on hover, source table/JSON view or download).
